title: What the role asks
hookLine: duties are measured by relationships: father, brother, neighbor (Enchiridion 30)
last: COUNT THE COST — FIRST, WHAT FOLLOWS.

lines: MY FATHER IS A BAD FATHER.
cards: A student comes to Epictetus with a complaint that sounds airtight. My father is a bad father. Surely that changes what I owe him.
People still bring that question to therapists, to clergy, to friends at two in the morning. The handbook's thirtieth section answers it with a short reply that has been argued over ever since.
It doesn't start with feelings, or with fairness. It starts with a relationship, and asks what that relationship, on its own, asks of you.

teach.b: Duties, Epictetus says, are measured by relationships. Is he a father? Then the role asks you to take care of him and give way to him.
But he's a bad father, says the student.

teach.h: NOT A GOOD FATHER. A FATHER.
teach.b: Epictetus answers: were you tied by nature to a good father? No. To a father.
Then the brother. Your brother treats you unjustly. Keep your own place toward him, Epictetus says.
Don't watch what he is doing; watch what you must do to keep your own choices in line with nature. And his usual hinge: no one can harm you unless you allow it.

The Stoics called a fitting act kathēkon, what's appropriate for this creature, in this place, in this relationship. The ancient biographer Diogenes Laertius says Zeno, the school's founder, first used the term.
Later Cicero turned it into Latin as officium, and wrote a whole book, On Duties, around it. That Latin word is the far ancestor of the English word office, a post with things you're expected to do.
The method: you'll find the duty of a neighbor, a citizen, a general, Epictetus says, if you get used to looking at the relationship itself.

teach.h: ASK: WHAT AM I TO THIS PERSON?
teach.b: Ask what am I to this person, and the next step usually shows up. One honest caution. Epictetus wrote that a son should bear even blows from his father, in a world that took that for granted.

Many modern readers of the Stoics add plainly that no role asks anyone to stay in danger, and protecting yourself is also a duty. What the chapter keeps is narrower: their failure doesn't erase your part.

how: People who practice Stoicism often think through their roles, as child, parent, friend, neighbor or worker, and ask what each one asks of them, rather than what the other person has earned.

o: a calm, settled mind that strong feelings can't shake
the fitting act: what a role or relationship asks of you
a duty owed only to people who treat you well

games.q: what the role asks — tap the pairs.

s: in Enchiridion 30, duties depend on whether the other person deserves them
Epictetus measures duties by the relationship itself: not a good father, a father.
Zeno is said to have first used the word kathēkon
Diogenes Laertius credits the founder of the Stoic school with the term.
Cicero wrote a book on duties built around this idea
On Duties, with officium as his Latin for kathēkon.

games.q: you tell Epictetus your father is a bad father. what does he say?
o: were you tied by nature to a good father? no, to a father.
games.why: the role is the measure: a father, not a good father. many modern readers add that no role asks anyone to stay in harm's way.

practice: Bring to mind the roles you hold this week, child, friend, neighbor, coworker, maybe parent, partner or sibling, and pick one.

Picture the person on the other side and ask quietly, not what they deserve, not what's fair, but what does this role ask of me today? Let one small answer come, a call, a dish washed, a word of thanks, and hold it.

wordCard.voice: Kathēkon. The Stoic word for the fitting act: what a role or relationship asks of you. Cicero called it officium, duty. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, a Stoic term: the fitting or appropriate act; Cicero's Latin is officium.

carryVoice: Your line: watch what you must do. The relationship tells you where to look. That's day three hundred sixty-two.

sources.ref: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 7.107–108
